Talk in detail about your core roles and: Group into clear buckets - infrastructure ownership (which platforms/services you own end to end), delivery (CI/CD, deployment processes you built or maintain), reliability (on-call, incident response, SLO ownership), and security/compliance if applicable - with one concrete example under each bucket rather than a flat list of tools, so the answer demonstrates actual scope and ownership.
Can you explain your current project usi: Pick one concrete application, describe its business purpose in a sentence, the scale it operates at (traffic, team size, criticality), and your specific role on it - grounding the answer in one real example is far more convincing than a general description of 'the project.'
Explain the infrastructure architecture: Walk top-down: how traffic enters (load balancer/ingress), the compute layer (GKE/Cloud Run and why), the data layer (database, cache), and supporting infrastructure (CI/CD, monitoring, security boundary) - a clear layered walkthrough signals you understand the whole system, not just the piece you touch most often.
Where does this application run?: State the specific runtime environment - which GCP project/region, GKE (Autopilot or Standard, cluster name/purpose) or another compute option, and any relevant environment separation (dev/staging/prod) - specificity here sets up the depth of follow-up questions correctly.
What are all the infrastructure componen: List systematically: compute (GKE cluster/node pools), networking (VPC, load balancer, DNS), data (database, cache, object storage), CI/CD (pipeline, artifact registry), and observability (monitoring, logging) - a complete list across these categories demonstrates you think about the full dependency graph, not just the application container itself.
Who decides the CPU and memory limits fo: Typically a collaborative decision - the application/development team proposes initial values based on load testing or profiling, and the platform/infrastructure team reviews them against cluster capacity planning and cost implications, adjusting based on observed production behavior (VPA recommendations, actual utilization data) rather than either side unilaterally deciding without the other's input.
How do you determine the CPU and memory: Start from load testing or observed production utilization data (never a guess) - set requests near the actual typical/steady-state usage (since requests drive scheduling and billing), and limits with headroom above typical peaks to absorb legitimate spikes without OOM-killing the container, while being cautious that a limit set far above requests can lead to noisy-neighbor CPU contention if many Pods burst simultaneously on the same node.
Does the application team also approve t: In a well-run organization, yes - resource sizing directly drives cluster capacity and therefore cost, so the application team (who understands the workload's actual needs) and the platform/cost-owning team both have a stake in the decision, ideally made visible through a shared cost dashboard rather than sizing decisions happening in isolation from cost awareness.
What resource quotas or limits do you co: ResourceQuotas at the namespace level (caps total CPU/memory/object counts a namespace can consume) and LimitRanges (enforces default and maximum request/limit values per Pod/container within a namespace, so a Pod can't be deployed with no limits at all or with unbounded resource requests) - these two together prevent any single namespace or workload from silently consuming unbounded shared cluster capacity.
How do CPU requests and limits work in K: The request is what the scheduler guarantees is reserved for the container when placing it on a node (used for scheduling decisions and, for HPA, as the denominator in utilization calculations) - a container can burst above its request if the node has spare CPU capacity. The limit is a hard ceiling - CPU is throttled (not killed) if the container tries to use more than its limit, since CPU is a compressible resource that can be rationed rather than needing to terminate the process.
What happens if a container exceeds its: The container is OOMKilled (terminated with exit code 137) immediately - memory is an incompressible resource, so unlike CPU there's no way to 'throttle' memory usage; the kernel simply kills the process once it exceeds its cgroup memory limit, and Kubernetes then restarts the container per its restart policy.

The container is throttled, not killed - the kernel's CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) bandwidth control restricts the container's CPU time to its limit over each scheduling period, which can manifest as increased latency/slower processing rather than a crash, since CPU (unlike memory) is compressible and can be rationed without terminating the process.
What is the difference between CPU utili: CPU utilization is a rate - how much processing time is being consumed over a period, which is compressible (a process can be throttled/slowed without crashing). Memory utilization is a stock - how much memory is currently held, which is incompressible (a process can't be 'slowed down' to use less memory; if it needs more than available, something must be killed) - this distinction is exactly why CPU limits throttle while memory limits kill.
How is memory different from disk storag: Memory (RAM) is volatile, extremely fast, and directly addressable by the CPU for active computation, but its contents are lost on power loss/restart. Disk storage is persistent (survives restarts/power loss) and much slower to access, used for data that needs to outlive a single process/container's lifecycle - this is why stateful data belongs on a PersistentVolume, not relied upon to survive in a container's in-memory state.
What monitoring tools do you use for the: Name the actual stack with the role each plays - Cloud Monitoring/Prometheus for metrics, Cloud Logging/ELK for logs, and Grafana for unified visualization - describing how they're actually used together (e.g. dashboards, alerting rules) rather than just a tool list.
Apart from native GCP monitoring, what t: Common answers include Datadog or New Relic for unified APM/infrastructure monitoring, PagerDuty/Opsgenie for alert routing and on-call management, and Prometheus/Grafana as an open-source alternative or complement to native Cloud Monitoring - naming the actual tools used and their specific role (not just that they exist) is what matters here.
What does Prisma Cloud monitor?: Prisma Cloud is a cloud security posture management (CSPM) and workload protection platform - it monitors cloud configuration for misconfigurations and compliance violations (overly permissive IAM, public storage buckets, missing encryption), scans container images and running workloads for vulnerabilities, and monitors network exposure and identity risk across the cloud environment.
Does Prisma monitor IAM security and net: Prisma Cloud's core strength is infrastructure/workload-level security - IAM, network exposure, container/image vulnerabilities, and compliance posture - rather than deep application-layer security testing (like SAST/DAST for custom application code logic flaws), which typically needs a dedicated application security tool alongside it; Prisma does extend into some application security via its WAAP module, but it's not a full replacement for application-specific security testing.
Have you worked on application security?: Answer honestly with specifics - which practices you've actually applied (dependency scanning, secure coding review, input validation, secrets management) versus areas you're less hands-on with (formal penetration testing) - a calibrated, honest answer is more useful than a blanket yes.
Have you worked on penetration testing o: Answer with actual scope - whether you've run vulnerability scans yourself (Trivy, Nessus) as part of a pipeline, or worked with results from a dedicated security team's penetration test, or have no direct experience here - being precise about the distinction between running a scanner and conducting an actual pentest matters.
Can you give an example of an applicatio: Describe a specific, real vulnerability you remediated - a dependency with a known CVE that needed patching, a misconfigured CORS policy, an exposed secret found via scanning - and the fix plus any prevention added (a new CI gate) - specificity is what makes this credible.
What are some important HTTP security he: `Strict-Transport-Security` (forces HTTPS), `Content-Security-Policy` (restricts what resources/scripts can load, mitigating XSS), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (prevents MIME-sniffing attacks), `X-Frame-Options`/`frame-ancestors` (prevents clickjacking), and `Referrer-Policy` (controls what referrer information is leaked to other sites) - each mitigates a specific, well-known class of web vulnerability.
What does Content Security Policy (CSP): CSP is a response header that tells the browser exactly which sources (scripts, styles, images, frames) are allowed to load and execute on a page, significantly reducing the impact of XSS attacks - even if an attacker manages to inject a malicious script tag, a properly configured CSP will block the browser from executing it if it doesn't originate from an allow-listed source.
How does Cluster Autoscaler work in Kube: Cluster Autoscaler watches for Pods that fail to schedule due to insufficient resources (Pending state) and, if a node pool could accommodate them, provisions new nodes to fit - and conversely, it identifies underutilized nodes whose Pods could be safely rescheduled elsewhere and removes those nodes (respecting PodDisruptionBudgets during the drain) to reduce cost. It operates purely on scheduling pressure, not on raw utilization percentage alone.
Do you have real-time monitoring for the: Answer with the actual setup - real-time dashboards (Grafana/Cloud Monitoring showing live cluster and workload metrics) backed by alerting rules that page on defined thresholds, versus only periodic manual checks - describing the actual alerting/dashboard configuration in place substantiates a 'yes' answer.
If there is a sudden spike in traffic, h: HPA reacts first (it polls metrics on a short interval, typically 15-30 seconds, and increases Pod replicas quickly if nodes have spare capacity) - but if there isn't enough node capacity for the new Pods, they go Pending, which then triggers Cluster Autoscaler to provision new nodes, a process that takes minutes (VM boot + node join + workload scheduling), not seconds - which is why a genuinely sudden spike can see a real gap between HPA wanting more replicas and actual capacity being available, best mitigated with some pre-provisioned headroom for latency-sensitive workloads.
I am referring to node autoscaling, not: Cluster Autoscaler monitors for unschedulable Pods (Pending due to insufficient node resources) and, if a configured node pool's max size hasn't been reached, provisions additional nodes matching that pool's machine type/configuration to fit them - and scales nodes back down when they become significantly underutilized and their workloads can be safely relocated elsewhere, all within the min/max bounds configured per node pool.
What happens if, due to some unknown iss: This typically means something is generating an ever-growing number of unschedulable Pods (a runaway job creation loop, a misconfigured CronJob spawning excessive Pods, or a bug causing repeated Pod recreation) - the Cluster Autoscaler is behaving correctly by trying to satisfy demand; the actual fix is identifying and stopping whatever is generating that unbounded Pod demand, not the autoscaler itself, though setting a sane `maxNodeCount` on the node pool acts as a critical safety ceiling to cap the cost/blast-radius impact while you investigate.
How do you control the cloud cost when C: Set a hard `maxNodeCount` per node pool as a non-negotiable cost ceiling, configure budget alerts that page when spend crosses a threshold so runaway scaling is caught within hours rather than at month-end billing review, and investigate the root cause of the demand (why are Pods being created faster than expected) rather than just capping the symptom - the max node count is a safety net, not a substitute for fixing whatever is actually generating unbounded resource demand.
